description:
SWE + CS students at Massey, Masters in Physics and Information Sciences. We are into space, tech and building random ideas into actual projects. We placed 2nd in NASA Space Apps 2025 with Exoplanet Explorer and we're back for another round.

Keen to meet some creative people who like problem-solving, trying weird ideas and building cool stuff. All skill levels welcome. 🚀
summary:
SPHERExPLORER is a web tool that lets anyone explore real NASA SPHEREx infrared data by blinking between observations of the same patch of sky taken months apart. Users pick a target by name or coordinates in a cinematic 3D space scene, fly to it, and see real SPHEREx images: one combined frame per visit, difference images, per-detector views, all 102 spectral channels, and a spectrum of the target.

Our Python pipeline fetches SPHEREx spectral image cutouts from NASA's IRSA archive, corrects target positions for proper motion, groups exposures by visit, aligns them on a common sky grid, and median-stacks them on one shared brightness scale so visits can be compared fairly. With it you can watch Barnard's Star move about 10 arcseconds in a year, see RW Aurigae dim between visits, and share a link to exactly what you found.

Comparing images over time has led to discoveries from Pluto to brown dwarfs. SPHERExPLORER puts that comparison in everyone's hands.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

SPHERExPLORER turns the SPHEREx all-sky survey into something anyone can explore. A user opens a planetarium-style 3D scene, opens the menu, and enters a target name or RA/Dec. The camera flies to the target while the data loads, then a viewer shows real SPHEREx images of that region:

- Blink: one combined frame per SPHEREx visit, played as an animation so motion and brightness changes stand out.

- Difference images between consecutive visits.

- Wavelength views: a false-colour composite (short to long infrared mapped blue to red), one stacked image per detector (6), and one image per spectral channel (102), using the official SPHEREx channel table.

- A spectrum of the target (aperture photometry on every exposure, plotted against wavelength), with saturated points flagged.

- A share link that reopens exactly the same view.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Data: SPHEREx Level 2 spectral image cutouts (IMAGE, FLAGS, VARIANCE, WCS-WAVE) from NASA/IPAC IRSA.

2. Positions: catalogue positions and proper motions (checked against SIMBAD) are propagated to each observation date, so fast movers stay centred.

3. Science pipeline (Python): drop unusable cutouts, mask bad pixels using the FLAGS bits, split exposures into visits, reproject every cutout onto a common tangent-plane grid centred on the target, median-stack each visit, then scale all visits with one shared brightness range so they are directly comparable.

4. API: a FastAPI service serves frames, differences, per-detector and per-channel images, spectra and target lookups. Demo targets are pre-computed for speed, with a live fallback.

5. Frontend: an ASP.NET Core (.NET 10) app proxies the API and hosts a Three.js/WebGL scene with a ray-traced black hole, nebulae, galaxies, an optional supernova intro and procedurally generated sound (Web Audio API).

RESULTS ON REAL DATA

- Barnard's Star: recovered its proper motion between SPHEREx visits (about 10 arcseconds over roughly a year; predicted and measured positions agree to within about half a pixel).

- RW Aurigae: its 4.6 micron brightness roughly halves between passes, a real variability signal.

- WISE 0855-0714 (one of the coldest known brown dwarfs) is not detected in single cutouts. We present that honestly as the limit of the data.

- Saturated stars (Barnard's Star core, R Draconis) are flagged in spectra as lower limits.

IMPACT

Volunteers have already found comets, brown dwarfs and other objects by comparing survey images. SPHERExPLORER makes SPHEREx's 102-colour infrared sky approachable for students, the public and citizen-science projects, and shareable links make it easy to point someone else at something interesting. The space scene is artistic; every image in the viewer is real SPHEREx data.

TOOLS

Python (FastAPI, Astropy, reproject, NumPy, Pillow), Docker and Render for hosting, C#/ASP.NET Core (.NET 10), JavaScript with Three.js (WebGL shaders), Web Audio API, GitHub.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Scientific honesty (no invented detail, no AI upscaling of data, saturation and non-detections are shown as such), fair comparison between visits (one shared brightness scale), speed on free hosting (pre-computed demo targets, slim deploy builds), performance on ordinary laptops (quality tiers with automatic fallback), and accessibility (skip controls, reduced-motion mode, no strobing).

USE OF AI TOOLS

We used Claude (Anthropic) to help write code, documentation and presentation material. The 3D visuals and sounds are generated procedurally by code at runtime, not by image or audio generation models.
